title: Machine Learning for the Design of Foundations on Rock Masses: A Critical Review of Data, Validation and Evidence Gaps
content: Machine-learning (ML) models are increasingly proposed for the bearing capacity of foundations on rock masses, but the evidence for design use has not been appraised for rock foundations specifically. This narrative critical review links the mechanics of foundations on Hoek–Brown rock masses to an appraisal of the ML studies that target them. Of 275 unique Scopus and Web of Science records screened by one reviewer, 48 addressed ML for foundations on rock (full texts read for 11); 21 studies are tabulated with their data origin, size and validation. The review is not systematic. Numerical data sets contain 80 to 5,120 runs, whereas field or literature-compiled data sets for rock-socketed piles and shafts contain 96–200 records. Sample counts and inputs recur across studies. One study generated Gaussian-noise records from its full 136-shaft set and then split the combined set 85/15; three studies tested on the same measured shafts without stating overlap with the training database, the latest using qu as an input although the target is Nσ = qu/σci. A three-level validation hierarchy is adapted to rock foundations. An illustrative synthetic experiment, not a bearing-capacity model, shows that row-wise random cross-validation of project-structured data can give R² ≈ 0.996, whereas grouped cross-validation gives 0.68 ± 0.14. An error of ±5 units in the Geological Strength Index changes the Hoek–Brown constant s by factors of 1.74 and 0.57. Within the sources examined, ML serves mainly as a surrogate for numerical solvers; independent generalization and field validity have largely not been demonstrated.
